question.prompt: A rectangular grid of squares has \(141\) rows and \(91\) columns. Each square has room for two numbers. Horace and Vera each fill in the grid by putting the numbers from \(1\) through \(141 \times 91 = 12{,}831\) into the squares. Horace fills the grid horizontally: he puts \(1\) through \(91\) in order from left to right into row \(1,\) puts \(92\) through \(182\) into row \(2\) in order from left to right, and continues similarly through row \(141.\) Vera fills the grid vertically: she puts \(1\) through \(141\) in order from top to bottom into column \(1,\) then \(142\) through \(282\) into column \(2\) in order from top to bottom, and continues similarly through column \(91.\) How many squares get two copies of the same number?

solutions.title: Write both cell values
solutions.explanation:
The number each person writes depends only on how many complete rows or columns come before the square. Counting those from zero makes the matching condition especially simple.

Let \(r\) be the number of rows above a square and \(c\) the number of columns to its left. Then
\[
0\le r\le140,\qquad 0\le c\le90.
\]
Horace has filled \(r\) complete rows of 91 squares before reaching this row, so he writes
\[
91r+c+1.
\]
Vera has filled \(c\) complete columns of 141 squares, so she writes
\[
141c+r+1.
\]
The two entries agree exactly when
\[
91r+c+1=141c+r+1,
\]
or
\[
90r=140c,\qquad 9r=14c.
\]
Since 9 and 14 have greatest common factor 1, the equation requires \(c\) to be a multiple of 9. Write \(c=9k\); substituting gives \(r=14k\). Conversely, every pair of this form satisfies the equation.

The bounds on the square become
\[
0\le9k\le90,\qquad 0\le14k\le140,
\]
so \(k\) can be any integer from 0 through 10. Each value gives one distinct square, and both endpoints are allowed. Therefore the number of matching squares is
\[
\boxed{11},
\]
choice \(\text{C}\).
